description.summary: Chroma is an open-source vector database and retrieval system that supports embedded local use, single-node serving, and distributed managed deployment.
description.description: Chroma stores embeddings, documents, and metadata and exposes vector similarity, metadata filtering, full-text and regex retrieval, and deployment-dependent sparse and hybrid search. Single-node Chroma uses HNSW, while Distributed Chroma and Chroma Cloud use SPANN over a multi-service architecture backed by a write-ahead log, object storage, local caches, and a SQL system catalog. This record distinguishes generally available collection APIs from Chroma Cloud Search API capabilities and from features that are not yet identical across local and distributed storage systems.

indexingConsiderations: Use local embedded mode for prototyping, single-node mode for moderate workloads, and distributed or Cloud mode when horizontal scaling and managed operations are required.
Tune HNSW only after measuring recall, latency, memory, build time, and ingestion behavior on representative embeddings.
Treat SPANN as a distinct distributed index whose configuration and storage behavior differ from single-node HNSW.
Disable unused full-text, regex, or metadata indexes where the deployment and schema support doing so, because every index increases write and storage cost.
retrievalConsiderations: Evaluate vector-only, lexical-only, sparse-only, and hybrid retrieval on a shared relevance set.
Keep local query APIs and Cloud Search API feature availability separate in application architecture.
Test selective metadata and document filters with realistic candidate counts and collection sizes.
Tune RRF weights and candidate limits rather than treating documented examples as universal defaults.

limitations: Single-node and distributed Chroma use different storage and indexing subsystems and do not yet have complete feature and behavior parity.
The composable Search API, sparse-vector schema, and documented RRF workflow are currently Chroma Cloud capabilities.
Single-node HNSW and distributed SPANN have different tuning, storage, scaling, latency, and recall tradeoffs.
Full-text containment search is case-sensitive, and regex or text predicates can increase indexing and query cost.
Metadata types and arrays have structural constraints, and cloud deployments impose request and collection quotas.
Local embedded deployments do not automatically provide the authentication, isolation, redundancy, scaling, or operational guarantees of Chroma Cloud.
Chroma does not expose general cross-collection or relational-style ACID transactions.
usageGuidance: Record the server and client versions because local, distributed, Search API, schema, and embedding-function behavior changes across releases.
Benchmark the intended deployment mode rather than extrapolating results between embedded HNSW and distributed SPANN.
Use tenant, database, and collection boundaries according to isolation, quota, lifecycle, and access patterns.
Monitor WAL ingestion, compaction, index freshness, cache behavior, object-storage reads, latency, and recall.
Maintain separate compatibility tests for local Chroma and Chroma Cloud whenever an application supports both.

claims.statement: Chroma supports embedded local, single-node, and distributed deployment modes; single-node collections use HNSW while Distributed Chroma and Chroma Cloud use SPANN, with squared-L2, cosine, and inner-product distance options.
claims.rationale: The architecture and collection-configuration documentation distinguish the three deployment modes and their HNSW or SPANN index implementations, metrics, and tuning scope.

claims.statement: Chroma supports metadata-filtered vector retrieval together with document full-text and regular-expression filtering.

qualifiers.name: filterScope
qualifiers.value: Metadata and document filters depend on indexed fields, supported operators, and deployment-specific limits

claims.rationale: The query documentation exposes metadata filters through where and document-content filters through where_document, including logical, containment, and regex operators.

claims.statement: Chroma supports dense and sparse vector retrieval and can combine retrieval channels through weighted Reciprocal Rank Fusion in the Chroma Cloud Search API.

qualifiers.name: availabilityScope
qualifiers.value: The composable Search API and sparse-vector hybrid workflow are documented for Chroma Cloud; equivalent single-node support is not yet fully available

claims.rationale: The sparse-vector and hybrid-search documentation shows dense and sparse KNN channels combined with configurable RRF weights, while the open-source roadmap documents temporary differences between distributed and local Chroma.

claims.statement: Distributed Chroma separates gateway, write-ahead log, query execution, compaction, system catalog, and object storage, and the log provides durability, replay, and atomicity across multi-record writes.

qualifiers.name: deploymentScope
qualifiers.value: Distributed Chroma and Chroma Cloud; operational topology and service management differ from embedded and single-node modes

claims.rationale: The distributed architecture documentation describes each service, the WAL acknowledgement path, object storage, SQL catalog, local SSD caches, and independently scalable runtime components.

claims.statement: Chroma organizes collections within databases and tenants, uses tenant-level isolation in its data model, and offers the distributed engine as a managed serverless Chroma Cloud service.

qualifiers.name: isolationScope
qualifiers.value: Tenant, quota, access-control, and billing behavior is most fully exposed in Chroma Cloud; local deployments require their own surrounding operational controls

claims.rationale: The architecture documentation defines tenant, database, and collection boundaries, while the Cloud and open-source pages describe the managed distributed service and current feature-parity boundaries.

evidence.summary: Official Chroma sources document local, single-node, and distributed modes, HNSW for single-node, SPANN for distributed deployments, and L2, cosine, and inner-product spaces.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can represent Chroma as a dedicated vector database spanning embedded, server, and distributed deployment styles rather than treating Chroma as local-only.
